key_insight: General-purpose LLMs could help extract psychosis symptoms from clinical notes for research, but they were only modestly accurate and struggled more with negative than positive symptoms.
clinical_relevance: This suggests LLM-derived symptom phenotyping may be useful for exploratory psychiatric research, but it is not yet reliable enough for clinical deployment.
method: Evaluated 14 general-purpose LLMs on extracting 8 schizophrenia symptoms from clinical summaries.
Tested both standard and few-shot prompting.
Compared LLM outputs with gold-standard labels and clinical-variable associations in a cohort of 704 patients.
evidence_signal: Across symptoms, performance ranged from poor to moderate, with macro F1 scores between 0.500 and 0.647, and positive symptoms were extracted more accurately than negative symptoms.
watch_item: Extraction errors, especially for negative symptoms, may create biased phenotypes and weaken or distort downstream analyses.
paper_title: Extracting Symptoms of Psychotic Disorders from Clinical Notes using Natural Language Processing.
